# DOSSIER 1 ANALYSIS — Writing & Linguistic Fingerprint

---

## NEW EVIDENCE READ

This dossier catalogues the full publicly known linguistic profile of Satoshi: consistent Commonwealth spellings and British idioms, a double-space typographic habit, formal academic register in the white paper, and the Aston University stylometric finding (Nick Szabo as closest match among 11 candidates). The dossier also flags an important methodological caution — stylometry on short technical corpora is contested and other analyses reached different conclusions. The omission of bit gold from the white paper's citations is re-noted as an analytical puzzle.

---

## ANALYSIS

**Hal Finney (deceased)**
The British spellings and idioms are a mild *inconsistency* with Finney's public profile as a California-raised American with no documented UK connection. His RPOW documentation and forum writing used standard American English. The double-space habit is ambiguous — it was common among anyone who used typewriters or early computing environments, which includes virtually all of our candidates. The Aston study reportedly did not rank Finney highly. Net effect: **slight downward pressure**.

**Nick Szabo (living)**
The linguistic evidence provides the strongest public signal here. The Aston University stylometric study — the only peer-reviewed forensic linguistics effort in the public record — ranked Szabo as the closest stylistic match to the white paper among 11 candidates. His blog writing ("Unenumerated") uses formal academic register, careful hedging, and dense technical prose highly consistent with the white paper's style. The *omission* of bit gold from citations cuts two ways: it could indicate Szabo avoiding self-citation to disguise authorship, or it could indicate a different author who simply prioritized citing directly technical predecessors. Neither interpretation is definitive. The dossier's methodological caveat appropriately limits how much weight we can put on the Aston study alone. Net effect: **upward pressure, but bounded by stylometric uncertainty**.

**Adam Back (living)**
The British spellings and idioms align with Back's confirmed status as a British cryptographer. This is a genuine positive consistency — he is one of very few candidates for whom British English is a natural first register. His technical writing (Hashcash paper, mailing list posts) also uses formal academic conventions. However, Back's publicly documented writing doesn't appear to have been specifically ranked highly in stylometric studies cited here. The fact that his Hashcash paper *is* cited while he claims minimal early involvement remains a documented tension in his profile — though not directly a linguistic one. Net effect: **modest upward pressure from British idiom consistency**.

**Wei Dai (living)**
Dai's b-money proposal and his publicly documented writing (LessWrong, Crypto++ documentation) are precise and technical. His writing has been characterized as somewhat more terse and less rhetorically developed than the white paper. No stylometric study in the public record ranked him as a top match. The b-money citation in the white paper (reference [1], the top billing) combined with the pre-publication email asking for citation details creates an interesting dynamic: if Dai were Satoshi, citing himself first would be either bold or accidentally self-revealing; if he isn't, it suggests genuine intellectual debt. Net effect: **neutral to slight downward**.

**Len Sassaman (deceased)**
Sassaman's professional writing — technical papers from COSIC, mailing list posts — was in fluent English but no specific stylometric analysis in the public record ranks him as a close match to the white paper. The European timezone argument is noted but is a behavioral, not linguistic, signal. His widow's statement that she saw no evidence of Bitcoin involvement is a soft inconsistency. Net effect: **neutral, no strong linguistic signal either direction**.

**Dorian Nakamoto (living)**
The Newsweek identification was not linguistically based, and nothing in this dossier supports his candidacy. His public statements showed uncertainty about Bitcoin itself. Net effect: **no change, remains very low**.

**Craig Wright (living)**
The UK High Court finding that Wright forged documents and lied extensively is directly relevant to linguistic evidence — it means any writing samples he has provided as "Satoshi" cannot be trusted as authentic. His Australian English is inconsistent with the British spellings (British and Australian English overlap somewhat, but specific idioms like "bloody hard" and "flat" for apartment are more distinctly British). The court ruling is itself strong evidence against him. Net effect: **no change, effectively eliminated by judicial finding**.

**Unknown / Not Listed**
The dossier's own methodological caveat is important: stylometry on short technical corpora is unreliable enough that different studies reached different conclusions. An unidentified British or Commonwealth-educated individual — or someone who deliberately adopted British conventions — cannot be ruled out. The 15% floor holds, and the genuine uncertainty in stylometric methods keeps this bucket relevant. Net effect: **stable at floor**.

---

## PROBABILITY BOARD

| Candidate | Probability | Key Driver |
|---|---|---|
| Nick Szabo | 28% | Aston stylometric study; bit gold conceptual match; academic register |
| Adam Back | 18% | British English consistency; Hashcash citation; first email contact |
| Hal Finney | 14% | RPOW precedent; first transaction; American English mild inconsistency |
| Unknown / Not Listed | 15% | Stylometric uncertainty; no cryptographic proof exists |
| Wei Dai | 8% | b-money citation #1; technical skill; not a strong stylometric match |
| Len Sassaman | 7% | Cypherpunk background; European timezone; no strong linguistic signal |
| Dorian Nakamoto | 5% | Name only; immediate denial; no technical or linguistic fit |
| Craig Wright | 5% | Judicially found not to be Satoshi; document forgery finding |

**Total: 100%**

> *Note: Craig Wright and Dorian Nakamoto retain non-zero probabilities only to acknowledge the limits of any external investigation, not because the evidence supports their candidacy.*

---

## WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS

The single piece of evidence that would most shift this board: **a direct, authenticated stylometric or authorship analysis comparing the full 80,000-word Satoshi corpus to confirmed private writing samples of the top candidates** — particularly unpublished emails, private correspondence, or draft documents that candidates could not have deliberately styled to match or diverge from Satoshi's voice. The Aston study used only public writing, which any sophisticated candidate could have adjusted. Private documents would dramatically increase or decrease confidence in any match.

---

## STANDING CAVEAT

This is a reasoning exercise grounded entirely in public evidence, and nothing in this analysis constitutes a determination — or even a strong implication — that any named individual is or is not Satoshi Nakamoto; that question remains publicly unresolved.

# DOSSIER 2 ANALYSIS — Timezone & Activity Patterns

---

## NEW EVIDENCE READ

This dossier presents converging behavioral evidence — forum timestamps, code commits, and mining patterns — all pointing to a consistent sleep window of approximately 05:00–11:00 UTC, most compatible with UK/GMT or US Eastern time zones, and explicitly inconsistent with the Japan claim on Satoshi's P2P Foundation profile. The Patoshi mining analysis independently corroborates the same daily off-window, suggesting the posting pattern reflects a genuine circadian rhythm rather than deliberate obfuscation. Crucially, the consistency *across three independent data streams* (posts, commits, mining) is stronger evidence than any single stream alone.

---

## ANALYSIS

**The core timezone finding and what it rules out / rules in**

Before candidate-by-candidate analysis, the structural finding deserves emphasis: three independent behavioral streams (forum posts, SourceForge commits, Patoshi mining) all show the *same* quiet window. This triple convergence makes deliberate schedule manipulation much less plausible — it would require Satoshi to have maintained a false sleep schedule across mining hardware operation, not just public communications. That is a meaningful constraint.

The compatible timezone bands are:
- **UK/GMT (UTC+0):** quiet window = roughly midnight to 6am local ✓ Clean fit
- **Western Europe (CET, UTC+1):** quiet window = roughly 1am to 7am local ✓ Reasonable fit
- **US Eastern (UTC-5):** quiet window = roughly midnight to 6am local ✓ Plausible for a normal schedule
- **US Pacific (UTC-8):** quiet window = roughly 9pm to 3am local — requires extreme night-owl behavior ⚠️
- **Japan (UTC+9):** quiet window = roughly 2pm to 8pm local — deeply inconsistent with any normal schedule ✗

---

**Hal Finney (deceased)**
Finney lived in Temple City, California — US Pacific time (UTC-8). The quiet window of 05:00–11:00 UTC corresponds to 9pm–3am Pacific. This is *possible* for an extreme night owl, but Finney's known health context complicates this: he was diagnosed with ALS in 2009, and someone managing a degenerative illness is perhaps less likely to be maintaining an extreme nocturnal schedule. His early Bitcoin involvement (January 2009) and the Patoshi mining window overlap create some tension — if Finney were Satoshi, his California location would require sustained late-night operation across posts, emails, and mining simultaneously. The public evidence is *mildly inconsistent* with Pacific timezone, though not disqualifying. Net effect: **modest downward pressure**.

**Nick Szabo (living)**
Szabo's documented location during this period is less precisely fixed in the public record — he has been based variously in the US and has connections to both coasts. If US Eastern-based, the timezone fits cleanly. However, no public evidence firmly places him in a GMT or CET timezone during 2008–2011. The timezone evidence is *conditionally consistent* with Szabo depending on where he was located — it neither strongly confirms nor disconfirms him relative to other US-based candidates. The Western holiday activity dip is consistent with any North American or European candidate. Net effect: **neutral, slight conditional upward if Eastern-based**.

**Adam Back (living)**
This is the clearest positive signal in this dossier for Back. He is a confirmed British cryptographer, UK-based for most of his career, placing him squarely in GMT/UTC+0 — the *cleanest* fit for the observed quiet window. A normal midnight-to-6am sleep schedule in London maps perfectly onto 00:00–06:00 UTC (or 05:00–11:00 UTC in winter, accounting for GMT). The triple convergence of posts, commits, and Patoshi mining all fitting a UK sleep schedule is *strongly consistent* with Back's confirmed geographic profile. The Western holiday pattern also fits a UK-based individual naturally. The public evidence here is the most directly consistent with Back among all named candidates. Net effect: **meaningful upward pressure — the strongest single-candidate signal in this dossier**.

**Wei Dai (living)**
Dai is US-based (Pacific Northwest, Washington state area, based on public records). This places him in US Pacific time — the same timezone problem as Finney. The quiet window 05:00–11:00 UTC = 9pm–3am Pacific, requiring persistent extreme night-owl behavior. His public writing style also tends toward terseness rather than the sustained engagement Satoshi showed. Net effect: **modest downward pressure from timezone mismatch**.

**Len Sassaman (deceased)**
Sassaman worked at COSIC, KU Leuven, Belgium — Central European Time (CET, UTC+1 in winter, UTC+2 in summer). This places his normal sleep window at approximately 23:00–05:00 UTC (CET) to 22:00–04:00 UTC (CEST). This is a *reasonable fit* with the observed quiet window, particularly in winter months when UTC+1 would map a midnight–6am local sleep to 23:00–05:00 UTC — close to but slightly offset from the 05:00–11:00 window. The fit is better than Pacific time but not as clean as pure GMT. Sassaman's European location was one of the primary arguments made in the 2021 essay proposing him as a candidate. This dossier gives that argument *modest but not strong* support. Net effect: **slight upward pressure, less than Back's**.

**Dorian Nakamoto (living)**
California-based, same timezone problem as Finney and Dai. The P2P Foundation "I am not Dorian Nakamoto" post, his immediate denial, and his established non-involvement in technical cryptography communities remain overwhelming inconsistencies. The timezone evidence adds another layer of inconsistency. Net effect: **no meaningful change, remains very low**.

**Craig Wright (living)**
Australia (AEST, UTC+10). The quiet window 05:00–11:00 UTC = 3pm–9pm AEST — Satoshi would have been asleep during Australian mid-afternoon, which is deeply implausible. This is actually *worse* than the Japan timezone problem the profile falsely claimed, and represents a strong behavioral inconsistency with Wright's Australian location. Combined with the judicial finding, this adds behavioral evidence against his claim. Net effect: **reinforces existing low probability**.

**Unknown / Not Listed**
The timezone analysis actually provides useful constraint here: it narrows the *Unknown* pool to UK/GMT, Western Europe (CET), or US Eastern-based individuals. This is meaningful — it reduces the geographic space of plausible unknown candidates. However, the triple convergence also raises the possibility of a disciplined, UK-educated person who has never been publicly identified. The 15% floor holds; the geographic narrowing doesn't eliminate this bucket. Net effect: **stable at floor, but geographic scope of unknown candidates usefully narrowed**.

---

## PROBABILITY BOARD

| Candidate | Previous % | Updated % | Key Driver |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nick Szabo | 28% | 25% | Timezone uncertain; US location slightly suboptimal vs. GMT |
| Adam Back | 18% | 24% | GMT location is cleanest fit; triple convergence directly consistent |
| Hal Finney | 14% | 11% | Pacific timezone requires extreme night-owl behavior |
| Unknown / Not Listed | 15% | 15% | Floor maintained; geographic pool narrowed to GMT/CET/EST |
| Wei Dai | 8% | 6% | Pacific timezone mismatch reinforced |
| Len Sassaman | 7% | 9% | CET is a reasonable fit; European timezone argument gains modest support |
| Dorian Nakamoto | 5% | 5% | California timezone adds to existing inconsistencies |
| Craig Wright | 5% | 5% | AEST is deeply inconsistent; judicial finding unchanged |

**Total: 100%**

---

## WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS

The single piece of evidence that would most shift this board: **a precise, verified location record for each top candidate during the period January 2009 – April 2011** — travel records, contemporaneous correspondence with timestamps and location metadata, or employer records placing a candidate in a specific timezone during Satoshi's active period. The entire timezone analysis rests on assumed residential locations; a candidate who was living or traveling in a different timezone than their "home base" would completely reframe these inferences.

---

## STANDING CAVEAT

This analysis draws exclusively on public behavioral and timestamp data and represents probabilistic reasoning about consistency and inconsistency, not a determination of any person's identity as Satoshi Nakamoto.

# DOSSIER 3 ANALYSIS — Code & Cryptographic Style

---

## NEW EVIDENCE READ

This dossier reveals that Bitcoin's original codebase was Windows-first with Microsoft-associated Hungarian notation conventions — strikingly unusual for the Unix-centric cypherpunk community — and that the cryptographic design combined non-standard but prescient choices (secp256k1) with an engineering-pragmatic approach that bypassed academic e-cash machinery entirely. The code shows a brilliant systems architect with likely industry rather than purely academic experience, and two-plus years of consistent, airtight operational security in version control. These are meaningful behavioral and technical fingerprints.

---

## ANALYSIS

**The Windows/Hungarian notation finding — the most underappreciated signal**

This deserves particular attention before candidate analysis. The cypherpunk community of 2008 was overwhelmingly Unix/Linux-oriented. For a cypherpunk insider to build Bitcoin's first release on Windows, with Microsoft-convention Hungarian notation, is genuinely anomalous. It suggests either: (a) the author had significant professional experience in Windows/Microsoft development environments, (b) the author came to cryptography from an industry software background rather than through the academic or Unix-native cypherpunk pipeline, or (c) both. This is a *cross-cutting constraint* that affects multiple candidates simultaneously, and it is one of the more concrete technical fingerprints in the public record.

**The secp256k1 choice — applied crypto awareness beyond academia**

Choosing a non-NIST Koblitz curve in 2008, when NIST P-256 was the overwhelming standard, indicates someone actively engaged with applied cryptography debates, aware of concerns about potentially manipulated NIST constants, but confident enough to deviate from convention. This points toward someone with strong independent cryptographic judgment, not a passive consumer of academic recommendations.

**The engineering-over-academia design philosophy**

Bypassing Chaum's blind signatures and academic e-cash machinery entirely, in favor of combining known engineering primitives, is a specific intellectual signature. The cypherpunk community *knew* about Chaumian systems — they were the dominant paradigm. Choosing not to use them wasn't ignorance; it was a deliberate architectural decision. This aligns with an engineer-practitioner mindset more than a pure academic one.

---

**Hal Finney (deceased)**
Finney presents a mixed picture here. As a PGP developer, he had deep C++ experience and worked in applied cryptography practically. His RPOW system was also a working implementation, not just a proposal, suggesting engineering capability. However, Finney was embedded in the Unix/PGP/open-source culture; his coding background was more aligned with that ecosystem than with Windows-first Microsoft conventions. No public evidence places him in a Windows-heavy development environment. The architectural choice to bypass Chaumian e-cash is interesting given Finney's known admiration for David Chaum's work — he would have had strong reasons to *include* blind signatures if he were designing from scratch. The public evidence here is *mildly inconsistent* with Finney as sole author. Net effect: **slight downward pressure**.

**Nick Szabo (living)**
Szabo's background is in law and computer science, and his writing is more academic-theoretical than engineering-practical. Bit gold was a *proposal* — it was never implemented. The code evidence cuts against a pure-Szabo authorship: the monolithic, industry-flavored, Windows-first codebase doesn't obviously match the profile of someone whose primary contribution is theoretical frameworks and blog essays. No public evidence places Szabo in Windows/Microsoft development environments. However, Szabo is clearly technically sophisticated, and the secp256k1 choice (independent cryptographic judgment, skeptical of NIST) aligns with his documented skepticism of government-influenced standards. Net effect: **modest downward pressure on sole authorship; the "brilliant systems design" doesn't match his public engineering profile as well as some competitors**.

**Adam Back (living)**
This dossier creates the most interesting tension for Back. On the positive side: his Hashcash implementation and cryptographic work show strong applied engineering skill, and his concern about NSA-influenced standards is well-documented and consistent with the secp256k1 choice. The decision to avoid academic e-cash machinery aligns with a pragmatic cryptographic engineer. On the negative side: Back's documented background is firmly in the Unix/open-source/academic cryptography tradition. The Hashcash paper and codebase were Linux-native. The Windows-first development with Hungarian notation is *inconsistent* with his known professional environment. This is a meaningful tension. The British timezone fit from Dossier 2 remains, but the coding environment evidence points away from him. Net effect: **modest downward pressure from Windows/Hungarian notation inconsistency**.

**Wei Dai (living)**
Dai is the author of Crypto++, a major C++ cryptography library — precisely the kind of serious, sustained C++ systems work that Bitcoin's codebase represents. Crypto++ is also cross-platform but has had significant Windows compatibility work. More importantly, Dai's background is in applied systems cryptography at an engineering level, not purely theoretical. His willingness to implement complex cryptographic systems from scratch in C++ is directly consistent with Bitcoin's codebase profile. The secp256k1 choice also fits someone deeply engaged with applied crypto primitives. The main question is the Windows-first platform — Dai's public work doesn't specifically indicate a Windows-primary environment, but his systems background is more consistent with it than the pure Unix cypherpunks. Net effect: **modest upward pressure — Crypto++ C++ work is the closest engineering match among named candidates**.

**Len Sassaman (deceased)**
Sassaman's work was in anonymity systems and applied cryptography (Mixmaster), with roots in the Unix-native privacy-tools community. His background is inconsistent with Windows-first development and Microsoft coding conventions. The decision to bypass Chaumian machinery is also somewhat inconsistent — Sassaman worked in a tradition (Chaum-influenced privacy systems) that might have pulled toward including such mechanisms. Net effect: **modest downward pressure**.

**Dorian Nakamoto (living)**
His background as a systems engineer on classified defense projects is interesting — defense contractors have historically used Microsoft environments extensively. However, the complete absence of any cryptographic sophistication in his public profile, combined with his denial and the judicial/journalistic consensus against the identification, makes this detail insufficient to raise his probability. Net effect: **no meaningful change**.

**Craig Wright (living)**
Wright has claimed various technical credentials, but the UK High Court found he forged documents extensively, making any technical claims he has made about his involvement deeply unreliable. His coding background has been publicly contested. The judicial finding remains the dominant evidence. Net effect: **no meaningful change**.

**Unknown / Not Listed**
This dossier actually expands the plausibility of the Unknown bucket in a specific way: the Windows-first, Hungarian-notation, industry-flavored profile points toward someone who might have come from *outside* the canonical cypherpunk academic pipeline — a professional software engineer with cryptographic interests who was never part of the known community. This is a profile that could easily belong to someone the public record has never surfaced. The operational security — two-plus years of perfectly scrubbed metadata — also suggests someone who understood exactly what they were doing and planned for permanent anonymity from the start. Net effect: **slight upward pressure; the "industry outsider" profile fits an unknown candidate well**.

---

## PROBABILITY BOARD

| Candidate | Previous % | Updated % | Key Driver |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nick Szabo | 25% | 21% | No public engineering profile matching Windows/industry codebase |
| Adam Back | 24% | 20% | Windows/Hungarian notation inconsistent with Unix-native background |
| Unknown / Not Listed | 15% | 18% | "Industry outsider" Windows-developer profile fits unidentified person |
| Hal Finney | 11% | 10% | Windows environment inconsistent; Chaumian avoidance awkward given his influences |
| Wei Dai | 6% | 9% | Crypto++ C++ engineering is closest public match to codebase profile |
| Len Sassaman | 9% | 8% | Unix/Chaum-influenced background inconsistent with code style |
| Dorian Nakamoto | 5% | 5% | No change |
| Craig Wright | 5% | 5% | Judicial finding unchanged; claimed technical credentials unreliable |

**Total: 100%**

---

## WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS

The single piece of evidence that would most shift this board: **a verified record of any top candidate's primary development environment during 2007–2009** — specifically, whether they were working day-to-day on Windows machines with Microsoft-ecosystem tools, or on Unix/Linux systems. This is the kind of mundane technical detail (employer IT records, contemporaneous screenshots, old hardware) that would either confirm or eliminate the Windows-Hungarian notation signal as a meaningful discriminator. It is also exactly the kind of detail that would be nearly impossible to fake retroactively.

---

## STANDING CAVEAT

This analysis reasons entirely from public evidence about coding conventions and technical choices, and constitutes probabilistic consistency-checking only — not an accusation or determination of any person's identity as Satoshi Nakamoto.

# DOSSIER 4 ANALYSIS — The Known Emails & Forum Posts

---

## NEW EVIDENCE READ

This dossier documents Satoshi's full arc of correspondence: initial contact with Back and Dai before the white paper, the cautious and methodical working relationships with early contributors, and a carefully managed exit triggered specifically by WikiLeaks attention and — most strikingly — Gavin Andresen's mention of a CIA/In-Q-Tel presentation. The correspondence pattern reveals a persona of extraordinary operational discipline who was not merely privacy-conscious in general but specifically alarmed by state-level attention, and who appears to have treated the CIA mention as a hard exit trigger. The final emails and the manner of handover are themselves behavioral evidence of considerable analytical weight.

---

## ANALYSIS

**The CIA/In-Q-Tel exit trigger — the most analytically significant detail**

This warrants emphasis before candidate analysis. Satoshi did not exit when Bitcoin became publicly prominent. He did not exit when Newsweek or mainstream press picked up the story. He exited *specifically* after Andresen mentioned presenting to In-Q-Tel, the CIA's venture arm. This is a precise and calibrated response, not general caution. The public evidence is consistent with someone who:

1. Had a specific, pre-existing reason to fear US intelligence attention — not just abstract privacy concerns
2. Understood institutional threat models at a sophisticated level
3. Was willing to abandon the project entirely rather than risk exposure to that specific class of attention

This narrows the psychological and situational profile considerably. It is consistent with someone who had professional experience with, or exposure to, intelligence/defense/government environments — or someone who had reason to believe their identity, if connected to Bitcoin, would attract investigation at that level.

**The Back/Dai first-contact sequence**

The email sequence (Back → Dai → white paper) is significant. Satoshi contacted Back *first*, asking about Hashcash. Back directed him to Dai. This ordering is consistent with someone who knew Hashcash well enough to want to cite it correctly, but did not already have a personal relationship with Back — otherwise a more direct conversation might have ensued. It is also consistent with someone who had independently developed Bitcoin's design using Hashcash as a building block, and was tidying citations post-facto rather than collaborating in real-time. The pre-registration of bitcoin.org before contacting Back or Dai further supports that the design was essentially complete before any outreach began.

**The methodical, impersonal correspondence style**

Every correspondent describes the same persona: technically confident, methodical, allergic to personal questions, entirely focused on the work. No voice, no face, no payment details across multiple years and multiple relationships. This is not casual privacy preference — it is sustained, professional-grade identity compartmentalization maintained under the social pressure of genuine working relationships. This level of discipline over years points toward someone with either training in operational security or an extremely high-stakes personal reason for anonymity.

---

**Hal Finney (deceased)**
The correspondence evidence creates a genuine puzzle for Finney's candidacy. He is documented as a *recipient* of Satoshi's communications — they debugged v0.1 together in January 2009, with Finney on the "other side" of the correspondence. If Finney were Satoshi, this entire documented exchange would be either fabricated (he was writing both sides) or involved a trusted intermediary. Finney published emails he claimed to have received from Satoshi; a writing-style analysis found differences. The "Satoshi and Finney corresponded" narrative is deeply embedded in the public record, and while a solo-performance or coordinated deception cannot be entirely ruled out, the public evidence here is *structurally inconsistent* with Finney as the sole author — it would require the most elaborate documented deception in the correspondence record. The CIA exit trigger is also less consistent with Finney's profile as a California-based open-source developer with no documented government/defense entanglements. Net effect: **downward pressure — the correspondence structure is awkward for Finney candidacy**.

**Nick Szabo (living)**
The CIA/In-Q-Tel exit trigger is worth examining against Szabo's profile. Szabo has documented interest in the legal and political dimensions of digital currency — his writing addresses state power, monetary sovereignty, and institutional trust extensively. A strong reaction to CIA-adjacent attention would be consistent with his worldview. However, Szabo's public profile doesn't include specific documented exposure to defense/intelligence environments that would make CIA attention a *personal* rather than merely philosophical threat. The correspondence style — methodical, impersonal, focused — is consistent with his known writing persona. His absence from the early Bitcoin community (he did not appear in the forums or mailing list discussions despite being the closest intellectual predecessor) is notable: if he were not Satoshi, one might expect him to have engaged; if he were, his absence is explained. Net effect: **broadly neutral; the exit trigger is consistent with his worldview but not specifically explanatory**.

**Adam Back (living)**
This dossier creates an interesting evidential texture for Back. He was Satoshi's *first contact* — but the email reads as a citation inquiry from someone who doesn't already know Back personally. This is either consistent with Back not being Satoshi (genuine first contact) or consistent with Back *being* Satoshi and constructing a paper trail that establishes apparent distance. The emails published in COPA v. Wright show Back responding helpfully but without evident prior familiarity. A key question the public record cannot answer: would a sophisticated operator like Back, if he were Satoshi, have deliberately created a "first contact" email trail with himself as a way of establishing an alibi in the correspondence record? This cannot be determined from public evidence, but it is worth noting as a structural possibility. The CIA exit reaction is notable: Back's work at Blockstream has involved institutional investors and he has operated openly in the industry since 2013 — somewhat inconsistent with someone who fled at the first hint of CIA attention. Net effect: **slight downward pressure from the CIA exit behavior, which sits uneasily with Back's subsequent public industry presence**.

**Wei Dai (living)**
Dai's position in the correspondence record is structurally similar to Finney's and Back's: he is a *recipient* of Satoshi's first outreach, not an initiator. If Dai were Satoshi, the pre-publication email asking for b-money citation details would be a constructed alibi — citing himself (reference [1]) while pretending to ask for the citation. Dai has publicly expressed regret at not engaging more with Satoshi at the time, which is either genuine (he wasn't Satoshi) or an extraordinarily committed piece of long-term misdirection. His subsequent low public profile is consistent with either interpretation. Net effect: **neutral; structural position in correspondence is ambiguous**.

**Len Sassaman (deceased)**
The correspondence evidence is perhaps most consistent with Sassaman's profile in one specific way: his death in July 2011, approximately two months after Satoshi's final emails, would explain the *permanent* nature of the silence in a way that living candidates require extraordinary ongoing discipline to maintain. If Sassaman were Satoshi, no ongoing deception would be required — the silence is simply death. The CIA exit trigger also fits: Sassaman was a privacy activist with documented concern about surveillance states, and In-Q-Tel attention to Bitcoin would represent exactly the kind of state-level threat that his professional worldview treated as serious. However, the correspondence style evidence — the years of sustained technical collaboration — would require that Sassaman maintained this elaborate persona while his colleague Meredith Patterson saw no evidence of it. Net effect: **modest upward pressure from death-explains-silence and CIA-threat consistency; partially offset by Patterson's testimony**.

**Dorian Nakamoto (living)**
Nothing in this dossier supports his candidacy. The sophistication of the correspondence, the Tor usage, the operational security, and the CIA-aware exit are entirely inconsistent with the public profile of a retired systems engineer who said he'd never heard of Bitcoin. Net effect: **no meaningful change**.

**Craig Wright (living)**
The judicial finding that Wright forged documents extensively means that any correspondence he has produced or claimed as evidence of Satoshi identity cannot be taken at face value. The COPA trial actually *published* authentic Satoshi emails (the Back/Dai sequence) as part of disproving Wright's claims — these authentic emails further establish a correspondence persona that is inconsistent with Wright's documented behavior (Wright's own communications have been described by the court as manipulative and grandiose, unlike Satoshi's methodical patience). Net effect: **no meaningful change; correspondence style is actually inconsistent with Wright's documented communication patterns**.

**Unknown / Not Listed**
The CIA/In-Q-Tel exit trigger is particularly relevant to this bucket. The specific, calibrated nature of the reaction — not fleeing from general publicity, but from *that particular* institutional attention — is consistent with someone who had personal rather than purely philosophical reasons to avoid US intelligence scrutiny. This could describe: a foreign national with concerns about US jurisdiction, someone with prior classified work creating conflict-of-interest concerns, someone involved in activities that would attract federal investigation, or simply someone with a very sophisticated threat model. None of the named candidates obviously fits this profile better than an unknown. The two-plus years of professional-grade operational security (Tor, anonymity email providers, scrubbed metadata across posts, commits, and mining) also points toward someone for whom this was practiced routine, not improvised caution. Net effect: **upward pressure — the exit trigger and operational discipline fit an unidentified sophisticated actor well**.

---

## PROBABILITY BOARD

| Candidate | Previous % | Updated % | Key Driver |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unknown / Not Listed | 18% | 22% | CIA exit trigger + operational discipline fit unidentified sophisticated actor |
| Nick Szabo | 21% | 20% | Broadly consistent; exit worldview fits; no specific new pressure |
| Adam Back | 20% | 17% | CIA exit behavior inconsistent with subsequent open industry presence |
| Wei Dai | 9% | 9% | Structural correspondence position ambiguous; no new pressure |
| Len Sassaman | 8% | 9% | Death explains silence; CIA threat consistent with his worldview |
| Hal Finney | 10% | 8% | Correspondence structure awkward for sole authorship; CIA exit less consistent |
| Dorian Nakamoto | 5% | 5% | No change |
| Craig Wright | 5% | 5% | Judicial finding + correspondence style inconsistency |

**Total: 100%** ✓

---

## WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS

# DOSSIER 5 ANALYSIS — Circumstantial & Social-Graph Links

---

## NEW EVIDENCE READ

This dossier synthesizes the macro-level constraints on the Satoshi question: the extremely small plausible author pool (estimated at a few dozen worldwide), the untouched ~1M BTC as a permanent behavioral signal, the universal denials from serious living candidates, and the unresolved group-versus-solo authorship debate. It also situates Bitcoin explicitly within the 2008 financial crisis and libertarian/cypherpunk ideological context. No single new smoking-gun fact emerges, but this dossier functions as a crucial integrative layer — it forces us to weigh the *cumulative* consistency of all prior dossiers against each candidate.

---

## ANALYSIS

**The untouched fortune — the most underweighted persistent signal**

Across five dossiers, this may be the single most analytically powerful fact. The ~1M BTC has never moved through price peaks at which it would represent tens of billions of dollars. Every living named candidate has therefore either:

1. Maintained superhuman financial restraint for 15+ years while watching that fortune fluctuate by billions
2. Lost the private keys
3. Is not Satoshi

Option 3 is the statistically parsimonious explanation for living candidates, but Options 1 and 2 cannot be eliminated. Critically, for *deceased* candidates, the silence is fully explained without requiring any ongoing restraint. This asymmetry is analytically significant and has been underweighted in public discourse.

**The plausible author pool is tiny**

The estimate of "a few dozen people worldwide" with the necessary combination of skills in 2008 is a strong constraint. Bitcoin required simultaneous mastery of: applied cryptography at implementation level, C++ systems engineering, distributed systems protocol design, economic mechanism design (incentive-compatible mining rewards), and sustained technical writing. This is not a profile that describes thousands of people. Every dossier has added constraints that further narrow this pool. The intersection of: correct timezone, Windows-development background, British English, cypherpunk ideological alignment, sufficient C++ depth, economic sophistication, and motive for extreme anonymity is a very small set.

**The denial pattern — what it does and doesn't tell us**

Every serious living candidate has denied being Satoshi. This is a complex evidential signal. On one hand, denials from people who have genuinely been falsely accused are expected. On the other hand, denial is also exactly what a rational Satoshi would do if they wanted to maintain anonymity. The denials are therefore *weakly exculpatory at best* — they cannot strongly raise or lower any candidate's probability, because both innocent and guilty parties have strong incentives to deny. The more meaningful observation is the *manner* of denial: Szabo's repeated, somewhat emphatic denials; Back's denials under oath-adjacent scrutiny; Dai's quiet non-engagement. None have produced cryptographic proof of non-involvement (which is impossible to produce), and none have produced cryptographic proof of involvement.

**The group-authorship question**

This dossier explicitly raises but doesn't resolve the group hypothesis. From the prior dossiers, the evidence cuts both ways:

*For solo authorship:* Single consistent coding style throughout v0.1, single consistent voice across 80,000 words, single Patoshi mining fingerprint, single operational security discipline maintained without any leak suggesting coordination.

*For group authorship:* The extraordinary breadth of skills, the flawless operational security (easier with explicit coordination), and the possibility that the "single voice" was one designated correspondent while others handled different components.

The public record cannot settle this. However, for probability purposes, group authorship increases the Unknown bucket's relevance — a group might well include someone never publicly identified.

---

**Hal Finney (deceased)**
The untouched fortune argument actually *helps* Finney's candidacy in death: a deceased Satoshi cannot move coins, explaining the permanent silence without requiring living restraint. His ALS diagnosis in 2009 and death in 2014 are documented. However, the social graph evidence cuts against him: if Finney were Satoshi, the entire documented correspondence relationship (Satoshi emailing Finney, Finney reporting bugs, Finney publishing emails he claimed to receive) would be an elaborate multi-year performance. The consistency of the persona described by *multiple independent correspondents* who interacted with both Satoshi and Finney separately makes solo deception increasingly strained. His known cypherpunk social embedding is entirely consistent with the ideological profile, and his RPOW work places him firmly in the lineage. But the correspondence structure remains the central difficulty. Net effect: **modest upward pressure from death-explains-coins; partially offset by correspondence complexity**.

**Nick Szabo (living)**
The social graph analysis is most pointed here. Szabo sits at the intellectual center of Bitcoin's lineage — his bit gold proposal is the closest conceptual predecessor, his writing articulates exactly the ideological motivations visible in the genesis block and P2P Foundation posts, and his stylometric profile is the closest forensic match in the public record. The omission of bit gold from the white paper, reconsidered here, is most parsimoniously explained in one of two ways: self-concealment (Szabo avoiding self-citation) or genuine non-authorship (a different author who didn't cite bit gold because they were already citing Back and Dai). Both remain live interpretations. For a living candidate, the untouched coins represent 15+ years of restraint or lost keys — extraordinary but not impossible for someone who understood from day one that moving the coins would be identifying. The financial crisis commentary in the genesis block and P2P Foundation posts matches Szabo's documented political-economic writing almost precisely. Net effect: **stable; remains the strongest single named candidate on accumulated evidence**.

**Adam Back (living)**
The social graph dossier adds one important contextual note for Back: he was the *first person Satoshi contacted*, and the domain registration and email addresses predate that contact. This means Back was Satoshi's first chosen interlocutor before any public announcement. This is consistent either with Back being Satoshi (constructing an alibi paper trail) or with Back being genuinely the most relevant person to consult first (Hashcash is architecturally central). The ideological profile — cypherpunk, privacy-focused, cryptographic libertarian — fits Back. However, the untouched coins issue is pointed for a living Back: he has been a public industry figure since 2013 as Blockstream CEO, operating openly, which is somewhat inconsistent with someone carrying the secret of a billion-dollar fortune in unreachable coins. This open, prominent public role since 2013 sits in mild tension with the CIA-exit profile from Dossier 4. Net effect: **slight downward pressure; public prominence since 2013 creates tension with Satoshi's permanent exit behavior**.

**Wei Dai (living)**
Dai holds a structurally unique position: he received the *first citation* in the white paper and pre-publication correspondence. If Dai were Satoshi, he cited himself first (reference [1]) while pretending to ask himself for citation details. This is logically possible but represents a highly convoluted construction. More naturally, the citation and correspondence reflect genuine intellectual debt. Dai's subsequent public behavior — quiet, low-profile, expressing mild regret at not engaging more with Bitcoin — is consistent with a genuine non-author watching a project he inspired grow enormously. The untouched coins would require extraordinary restraint from a living Dai. His technical skills (Crypto++, C++) remain the closest engineering match to the codebase. But the social graph evidence, on balance, points toward genuine non-authorship. Net effect: **slight downward pressure from social graph structure; skills evidence remains the counterweight**.

**Len Sassaman (deceased)**
This dossier strengthens the Sassaman candidacy modestly in one specific dimension: the combination of (a) death explaining the coin silence, (b) timing of death closely following final Satoshi communications, (c) cypherpunk social embedding, and (d) ideological alignment with the crisis commentary and privacy motivations. However, the social graph cuts against him in an important way: Sassaman was not cited, not contacted, and not mentioned in any of Satoshi's known correspondence. Every person Satoshi contacted (Back, Dai, Finney, later Andresen and Hearn) has a documented connection to specific technical components of Bitcoin. Sassaman's specialty (anonymous remailers, Mixmaster) has no direct technical analog in Bitcoin's design — Bitcoin is notably *pseudonymous*, not anonymous in the Sassaman/Mixmaster sense. This is an underappreciated inconsistency. Net effect: **slight downward pressure from absence in social graph and technical-specialty mismatch**.

**Dorian Nakamoto (living)**
The social graph analysis makes his candidacy essentially untenable. He has no presence in the cypherpunk lineage, no connection to any cited work, no documented cryptographic or C++ background at the required level, and no ideological alignment with the libertarian financial commentary. He shares a name and a neighborhood with Finney. That is the entirety of the public evidence supporting his candidacy. Net effect: **no meaningful change; remains a floor candidate**.

**Craig Wright (living)**
The judicial finding is reinforced by the social graph analysis: the COPA trial specifically examined the authentic correspondence record (Back/Dai emails) and found it incompatible with Wright's claims. His position in the cypherpunk social graph prior to 2008 is not documented in the public record in a way that would explain Satoshi's intimate knowledge of the lineage. Net effect: **no meaningful change**.

**Unknown / Not Listed**
The social graph analysis is, paradoxically, where this bucket gains its most compelling support. The combination of constraints — tiny author pool, specific skills intersection, British English, Windows development, GMT timezone, CIA-aware exit, 15+ years of coin silence, zero metadata leakage across two years — describes someone who left essentially no public trace. The group-authorship hypothesis also lives primarily here: a collaboration between a known and an unknown figure, or between two unknown figures, cannot be excluded. Fifteen years of investigation by motivated journalists, academics, and cryptographers with strong financial incentives to solve this have produced no confirmed answer. That outcome is itself evidence about the difficulty of the problem and the sophistication of the concealment. Net effect: **upward pressure; cumulative constraints point toward a highly capable, possibly unknown actor**.

## CUMULATIVE SYNTHESIS ACROSS ALL FIVE DOSSIERS

After five dossiers, the public evidence is most consistent with a **small set of overlapping profiles**:

- A writer of British or Commonwealth English, likely GMT-timezone based
- A skilled C++ engineer with Windows/industry (not purely Unix/academic) development background
- Someone deeply embedded in the cypherpunk ideological tradition with specific knowledge of the Back/Dai/Szabo/Finney lineage
- Someone with a sophisticated, pre-planned operational security posture — not improvised anonymity
- Someone specifically alarmed by US intelligence attention (the CIA/In-Q-Tel trigger)
- Someone who either died, lost their keys, or has maintained extraordinary restraint with ~1M BTC

**No named candidate fits all these criteria cleanly.** Szabo fits the intellectual and stylometric profile best; Back fits the linguistic and timezone profile best; Finney and Sassaman fit the "death explains silence" criterion; Dai fits the engineering profile best. The Unknown bucket reflects the honest possibility that the actual author threads these needles in a way the public record has not yet surfaced.

This is the only evidence that would be genuinely dispositive — it is also the only evidence that Satoshi, if living and disciplined, has specifically chosen never to produce. Its continued absence is itself the most important single fact in the entire public record.
